analysis.one_liner: Makes companies that handle hazardous substances prove they can pay for toxic site cleanups before going bankrupt.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by three Senate Democrats in 2007 and never received a committee vote or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Superfund law, the companies responsible for toxic contamination are supposed to pay for cleanup. But when those companies go bankrupt or shuffle assets to parent or affiliate companies, cleanup costs often fall to taxpayers. This bill would have forced the EPA to finally write rules — required by a 1980 law but never issued — requiring hazardous-substance handlers to show proof of financial ability to cover cleanup costs, required companies to notify the EPA when they file for bankruptcy, and allowed bankruptcy trustees to claw back assets moved within 10 years to dodge environmental liabilities.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who currently cover cleanup costs when polluting companies default or reorganize in bankruptcy; and people living near the 1,244 Superfund sites on the National Priorities List, whose cleanups would be faster because money would be secured up front.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and residents near toxic sites

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the EPA to finish, within 18 months, financial assurance regulations under CERCLA section 108(b) — a rulemaking Congress mandated in 1980 that the EPA had never completed — requiring facilities to prove they can pay for potential cleanups. [S2] [S3]

Companies in regulated classes that file for bankruptcy would have to notify the EPA and disclose estimated environmental impacts and their corporate relationships, closing the information gap a 2005 GAO report identified. [S2] [S3]

Bankruptcy trustees could unwind transfers of assets made within 10 years before a bankruptcy filing if the debtor had environmental liabilities and moved assets with intent to hinder, delay, or defraud — extending the standard lookback period. [S2] [S3]

The bill's findings cite an average taxpayer cost of $12 million per Superfund site cleanup and state that taxpayers increasingly cover costs because polluters are no longer taxed for that purpose. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Companies that produce, transport, treat, store, or dispose of hazardous substances, which would bear the cost of demonstrating and maintaining financial assurance for cleanup obligations, and any corporate parents that previously could shed environmental liabilities through asset transfers or bankruptcy reorganizations.

drawbacks.text: Financial assurance requirements impose real compliance costs on facilities handling hazardous substances, and those costs could be passed to consumers or discourage some operators from continuing to handle such substances. [S3]

The 10-year clawback provision reaches further back than standard bankruptcy law, which could complicate ordinary corporate restructuring, though it applies only to transfers made with intent to defraud environmental creditors. [S3]

The bill is largely a mandate to the EPA to complete a long-delayed rulemaking; it does not itself guarantee cleanups get funded, and its effectiveness depends on how strict EPA writes and enforces the rules. [S2] [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — ending the practice of polluting companies escaping cleanup costs through bankruptcy, leaving taxpayers with $12-million-per-site bills — is substantial and directly enforces the polluter-pays principle. The compliance costs fall on the companies that create the hazardous-substance risk, which is the point, though smaller operators could find the assurance requirements burdensome and the bill's real-world effect depends entirely on EPA writing and enforcing strict rules. On balance the design is straightforward and targeted.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it sat there until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Maria Cantwell introduced the Cleanup Assurance and Polluter Accountability Act on January 31, 2007, joined by Senators Boxer and Lautenberg. [S1] [S3]
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day of introduction — the only action it ever received. [S5]
The bill had two cosponsors in addition to the sponsor, all Democrats, and no further action, hearings, or votes are recorded before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009. [S4] [S5]

The bill's own findings note the EPA had failed for more than 25 years to implement the 1980 statutory mandate to require proof of financial ability to pay for cleanups, which is what the bill was designed to force. [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that produce, transport, store, or dispose of hazardous substances are better off because the bill died — they never had to prove financial ability to cover cleanup costs, and the EPA was never forced to finish the regulations Congress ordered in 1980. The cost of cleanups when polluting companies default continues to fall on taxpayers.

for.name: Maria Cantwell
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Barbara Boxer and Frank Lautenberg
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsoring senators were Democrats; the record shows no Republican support and no recorded opposition votes because the bill never reached the floor.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers and hazardous waste handlers
industries.note: The bill would have required these facilities to prove financial ability to cover Superfund cleanup costs, ending their ability to escape liability through bankruptcy or corporate restructuring. Today, when such companies default, taxpayers pick up the cleanup bill. [S2] [S3]

industries.industry: Corporate parents and affiliates of polluting companies
industries.note: The bill would have extended the bankruptcy clawback window to 10 years for asset transfers intended to dodge environmental liabilities, and required bankrupt facilities to disclose all parent, subsidiary, and affiliate relationships to the EPA. [S2] [S3]
Facilities would have needed financial assurance instruments to satisfy the requirements, creating demand for insurance, surety bonds, and guarantee products. [S3]
